title: He Played Cricket as a Teenager. On Thursday in Rome, He Threw 92.62 Metres and Went Past Neeraj Chopra's Asian Record.
excerpt: Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage is now the second-best Asian javelin thrower in history. India's Sachin Yadav, meanwhile, finished eighth on his Diamond League debut.
body:
Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage was once a promising fast bowler in Sri Lanka's cricket system. He reportedly clocked 134 km/h as a teenager. At some point, he decided the javelin suited him better than the cricket ball. On Thursday evening in Rome, that decision looked like one of the finest in Sri Lankan sporting history.

Pathirage threw 92.62 metres in the second round of the Diamond League Golden Gala Pietro Mennea — a distance that shattered the meeting record, established the 2026 world-leading mark, and vaulted him past both Chinese Taipei's Chao-Tsun Cheng (91.36m) and India's Neeraj Chopra (90.23m) to become the second-best Asian javelin thrower of all time.

Only Arshad Nadeem's Olympic gold-winning 92.97m from Paris 2024 now stands above him on the Asian all-time list. Pathirage also became the fourth Asian — and the 28th athlete in history — to cross 90 metres.

## A season that changed everything

The 23-year-old's trajectory in 2026 has been staggering. He entered the year with a personal best of 85.45m. In March, he threw 89.37m at a domestic meet, immediately establishing himself as the world season leader. He won the Kip Keino Classic in Nairobi with 89.28m. He finished second at the Rabat Diamond League on May 31 with 85.97m.

Then came Rome. His opening throw was a solid 84.49m. His second was 92.62m — an improvement of more than eight metres between attempts, the kind of jump that makes commentators reach for superlatives and rivals recalibrate their seasons.

The winning margin was extraordinary. Anderson Peters, the two-time world champion and Paris Olympics bronze medallist from Grenada, finished second — nearly nine metres behind, at 83.91m. American Curtis Thompson was third at 83.89m. World champion Keshorn Walcott ended fourth.

## What it means for India

Two Indian storylines emerged from Rome, neither of them comfortable.

First, Neeraj Chopra's Asian record of 90.23m — set during his World Championship gold in Budapest in 2023 — is no longer the continent's second-best mark. Chopra remains India's greatest track and field athlete, with two Olympic medals and a World Championship crown. But the javelin landscape has shifted. A 23-year-old from Sri Lanka who was playing cricket five years ago now throws farther than he ever has.

Chopra, who is currently training in Bienne, Switzerland after a stint in Türkiye, did not compete in Rome. It is not yet known when he will begin his competitive season. The Neeraj Chopra Classic in Bengaluru on July 5 and the Diamond League finale in Zurich are among his expected appearances.

Second, India's Sachin Yadav had a difficult Diamond League debut. The 26-year-old, who finished fourth at the 2025 World Championships with a personal best of 86.27m, managed only 79.18m in Rome — finishing eighth in a 10-man field. His five throws read 79.18m, 77.02m, 76.62m, and 75.54m after an opening foul. He did not qualify for the final round.

## The bigger picture for Indian athletics

Indian javelin has been a Chopra-centric story since Tokyo 2021. Kishore Jena's emergence in 2023 added a second name, but the depth beyond them remains thin. Yadav's Rome outing was a reminder that competing at Diamond League level requires more than a good personal best — it requires big-stage composure and consistency under elite conditions.

Pathirage's breakthrough also underscores how quickly the javelin world moves. A year ago, the Sri Lankan was not in the conversation for podium finishes at Diamond League meets. Now he sits eighth on the all-time world list and will enter the World Championships in Tokyo next month as one of the clear favourites.

The next Diamond League meeting featuring men's javelin is in Doha on June 19. Whether Chopra enters remains uncertain, but the conversation has changed. The Asian javelin crown is no longer India's alone.
